verses.translation_literal: A prayer, of David. Incline, YHWH, your ear; answer me, for poor and needy [am] I.
verses.translation_dramatic: A prayer. David's. Lean down, LORD, and bend your ear to me. Answer me. For I am poor, and I am needy, I who stand before you with nothing in my hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a beggar at a gate, not a petitioner at a banquet. "Incline your ear" is a picture of a great one stooping to a small voice, and it sets the posture for the whole psalm: the speaker is low, God is high, and the only claim he can make is his need. The command is blunt, and the Hebrew is blunter than it sounds in English: ʿăneni is the imperative "answer me", a plea for a reply, not just a hearing. The KJV weakens it to "hear me"; the ASV and YLT keep the stronger "answer me". Listening is not enough for him. He wants the LORD to respond.

There is a quiet sound-play in the verse. The verb "answer" (ʿănēnī, root ʿ-n-h) and the word "poor" (ʿānī) are written almost alike: ʿăneni, kî ʿānî. The one who needs an answer is the one who is ʿānî, and the ear is bent toward him for that reason. "Poor" (ʿānî) points to someone bowed down, afflicted, without resources; "needy" (ʾevyôn) to someone who lacks and begs. Together they were a stock pair for the vulnerable, and Radak reads the doubling as a strengthening of the claim. The closing "I" is emphatic: poor and needy, I. The Hebrew puts the pronoun last, so the line ends on the speaker himself. The title "A prayer of David" is part of verse 1 in the Hebrew and is simply unnumbered in the KJV, which is why the two numberings agree here.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of the verb 'to stretch, bend, incline'. With 'ear' it is the idiom for attentive listening, picturing someone leaning down toward a speaker. Metzudat David glosses it as listening to the prayer and answering.
Imperative of ענה 'to answer' plus 'me'. It asks for a reply, which is stronger than the KJV's 'hear me'. It also sounds like the next key word עָנִי 'poor'.
A paired expression for the poor and defenseless. Meiri says אביון is added because the language habitually joins it to עני; Radak reads the doubling as strengthening the plea.

verses.translation_literal: Guard my life, for loyal [am] I. Save your servant, you [are] my God, the one trusting to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Guard my life, for I have kept faith. Save your servant, you who are my God, your servant who has put all his trust in you.
verses.directors_commentary: Two commands, two reasons. 'Guard my life' (נפשי) means my whole self, my breath, my neck; it is what an enemy threatens. 'Loyal' (חָסִיד) is the heart of the verse and the KJV mistranslates it: 'holy' suggests sanctity or ritual purity, but the word is the person who practises חסד, covenant faithfulness, who repays loyalty with loyalty. Radak says David means he did no harm to those who harmed him, and that is what makes the claim bearable; Rashi and Meiri quote the old teaching about the man who hears insult, could take revenge, and stays silent. Do not play it as pride. 'Servant' (עבד) is a standing: a man who belongs to a master and can therefore claim protection. The last phrase 'the one trusting to you' uses 'to' (אל) rather than 'in', which Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all read as 'in you', so the KJV's 'that trusteth in thee' is fine, though it reorders the clauses.

philological_notes.note: One who lives by חסד, covenant loyalty; not 'holy' (קדוש). Rashi, Radak and Meiri each discuss why David may call himself this: he returns good for evil and does not take revenge.
A long-vowelled imperative 'guard!', not a perfect. The lengthened form is for the melody, per Radak.

verses.translation_literal: Show me favor, Lord, for to you I call all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, Lord. All day long, I am calling to you.
verses.directors_commentary: From here the psalm names God 'Adonai', 'my Lord', the title of a master, a word that fits the 'servant' of verse 2. The Hebrew verb חנן is not 'be merciful' in the sense of pity alone; it is the favor a superior grants freely to someone with no claim. The KJV's 'daily' flattens 'all the day' (כל היום): the petitioner calls from dawn to dusk, without stopping. Ibn Ezra says it plainly: I have nothing else to do but call. Rashi, relaying the Aggadah, reads 'all the day' as the whole exile, which is day for the nations and night for Israel. The speaker is not expecting an answer yet; he is wearing the door down.

philological_notes.note: 'Be gracious to me', a favor given freely, unearned. Linked in sound to תחנונותי in verse 6.

verses.translation_literal: Gladden the life of your servant, for to you, Lord, my life I lift.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make glad the soul of your servant. For to you, Lord, I lift my soul, and I hold it up in both hands.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Life' (נפש) occurs twice in one line, once in God's hands to be cheered and once in the speaker's hands to be raised. Keep the repetition audible. The image 'I lift up my life' is concrete: you carry something up to someone as an offering, or hand your burden to a stronger person. Meiri takes it as bringing an offering (like a gift carried to a host, Gen 43:34) and Metzudat David as loading oneself on God to lean on him; Radak allows prayer, offering or hope. The KJV's 'Rejoice the soul' is archaic and can read as 'celebrate'; the Hebrew is an imperative to make glad. The request is modest: not rescue yet, but gladness for a person who is grieving (Radak: 'in sorrow and sighing').

philological_notes.note: 'I lift my life': the same idiom of orienting the whole self toward God appears in Psalm 25:1 and 143:8, and elsewhere can also mean to long for something. Ancient readers give three senses: hope, an offering, or a burden placed on God.

verses.translation_literal: For you, Lord, [are] good and forgiving, and abundant of loyal love to all who call you.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you, Lord, are good, and quick to forgive, and your steadfast love runs deep for everyone who calls to you.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason the psalmist dares to ask, and it echoes the old formula of Exodus 34:6, 'abundant in חסד'. The unusual word is סַלָּח, 'forgiving', which is an adjective, not a verb: it names a trait, as if forgiveness were part of God's character, not a decision. It occurs only here in the Bible, and the KJV's 'ready to forgive' is a good guess at that. 'Chesed' (חסד) is the same root as the 'loyal' of verse 2: the speaker claims to share the quality he asks for. 'To all who call you' sets no condition of merit. Ibn Ezra splits the verse: good to the good, forgiving to sinners; Malbim says God's gift never depends on the receiver's deeds, only on his chesed.

philological_notes.note: An adjective of settled character, 'forgiving', found only here in the Hebrew Bible; elsewhere the verb סלח is used with God as subject.
'Abundant in covenant love', part of the confession in Exodus 34:6. It links to the 'chasid' of verse 2.

verses.translation_literal: Give ear, YHWH, [to] my prayer, and pay attention to the sound of my supplications.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me, LORD, hear my prayer. Listen to the sound of my pleading.
verses.directors_commentary: The first verse's request returns, now in a new key: the speaker has said who God is and now asks again. Hebrew has two near-synonyms for hearing here, האזין ('use the ear') and הקשיב ('prick up the attention'), which build a crescendo from the opening 'incline the ear'. 'The sound of my supplications' (קול תחנונותי) is literally the voice: the plea is a noise God is asked to pick out. Malbim distinguishes תפלה (the soul's rising above the body) from תחנונים (bodily requests). The KJV gets it nearly right; 'voice' and 'sound' are both fine for קול.

philological_notes.note: Plural of תחנון, 'pleas for favor', from the root of 'be gracious' (חננו) in verse 3, so this verse answers the earlier request.

verses.translation_literal: In the day of my distress I call you, for you answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the day my trouble closes in, I call to you, because you will answer me.
verses.directors_commentary: The ancient idea of a 'day of distress' (צרה, from a root meaning narrow) is a day when the walls close in: war, illness, famine, a false charge. The last clause closes the circle with verse 1: he began 'answer me' (ענני) and ends with 'you will answer me' (תענני), the same word, so the plea becomes certainty. The imperfect verb can be 'you answer' or 'you will answer'; the KJV's 'will call' and 'wilt answer' are fair. Radak sets this up as a polemic: other gods are called on and do not answer, which prepares verse 8. Ibn Ezra adds that he is not testing God; he calls because he is truly in trouble.

philological_notes.note: 'You answer me'; picks up 'answer me' (עֲנֵנִי) from verse 1, so the psalm's first request becomes its stated confidence.

verses.translation_literal: There is none like you among the gods, Lord, and there is none like your works.
verses.translation_dramatic: Among the gods there is none like you, Lord, and no deed to set beside your deeds.
verses.directors_commentary: This is an ancient way to claim the highest title: in the Near East every city had its gods, and a worshipper praised his own as unmatched. Israel's poets use the same form, but the claim is edgier because in the surrounding religions the 'gods' ran the sun, the moon, storms and seas. The Hebrew says 'among the gods' (באלהים) and does not say whether they exist; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take them as powers or heavenly beings who do only what they are commanded, or the stars that the nations worship. The KJV's 'Among the gods' is right, but its 'neither are there any works' adds an English 'any' that softens the stark 'and none like your works'. Hear the double 'none' (אין... ואין) as two hammer blows.

philological_notes.note: 'Among the gods'. The commentators read the plural as the beings other peoples called gods: stars, angels, heavenly officers. Meiri says Scripture calls them 'gods' by their worshippers' idea of them.
'There is none like you': the same incomparability formula as Exodus 15:11, 'Who is like you among the gods, YHWH?'

verses.translation_literal: All nations which you have made will come and bow down before you, Lord, and will honor your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: All the nations you have made will come, Lord. They will bow low before you and give honor to your name.
verses.directors_commentary: A startling picture from the mouth of a man in danger from foreigners: the nations that now threaten him will one day walk to God as pilgrims. Note 'which you have made': because the Lord made them, they are his to call. The verbs are imperfect, so 'will come' and 'let them come' both work; I kept the future. 'Bow down' (השתחוה) is the full prostration of a subject before a king, which is why the KJV's 'worship' is a little vague: the Hebrew is a body movement, face to the ground. 'Honor' (כבד) is from the root 'to be heavy', giving weight to the name. Radak and Meiri place this at the time of the Messiah; Ibn Ezra says the nations will tell how God saved a poor man, so God's rescue of one person preaches to them.

philological_notes.note: Bow down, prostrate: a body gesture of homage before a superior, before 'before you' (לפניך), the face of the king.
'Give weight to, honor': the root means 'heavy', as in giving glory (כבוד) weight.

verses.translation_literal: For great [are] you, and doing wonders; you [are] God, you alone.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are great, and you work wonders. You, and you alone, are God.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'for' gives the reason the nations will come: they will see his wonders (נפלאות), acts beyond ordinary human expectation, such as the Exodus. 'Doing wonders' is a participle, a continuing activity, not a single past act; the KJV's 'doest wondrous things' gets that. The sharpest phrase is 'you alone' (לבדך), which in the Hebrew sits at the end, sounding like a closing door. Radak says the nations will recognize this when God brings Israel out from among them. Rashi cites the Aggadah that the heavens and the earth were made before the angels. Ibn Ezra imagines the nations denying their own gods. 'Great' (גדול) is a royal word, as in 'the great king'.

philological_notes.note: 'Wonders', acts that exceed what is expected or possible; the word used for the plagues and the sea-crossing in the Exodus tradition.
'You alone', literally 'to your separateness'; the claim of sole divinity.

verses.translation_literal: Teach me, YHWH, your way; I will walk in your truth. Unite my heart to fear your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach me your way, LORD, and I will walk in your truth. Make my heart one, undivided, to revere your name.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood shifts from praise back to need: after naming who God is, the speaker asks to be shaped to him. 'Way' (דרך) is a road, a way of life; 'truth' (אמת) is also reliability, faithfulness, so 'walk in your truth' means to walk steadily on the ground God has made firm. The key request is 'unite my heart' (יחד לבבי): the heart is the seat of thought and will, and the plea is for a heart with one focus instead of two. Meiri reads two competing impulses; Metzudat David, a single mind not hanging in doubt. YLT's 'rejoice' misreads the verb. 'Fear' (יראה) is not terror but awe and obedience; the KJV's 'fear' is accurate, and BBE's 'glad' is not in the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra notes the verb is from יחד, 'together' or 'one'.

philological_notes.note: 'Make my heart one, gather it', with a divided heart as the opposite of a united one. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion derive it from אחד / חד. The doubled-ב form לבבי is the full word for 'heart', sometimes taken to hint at two inclinations.
'Your truth' as faithfulness and firmness, not only factual accuracy.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to you, Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will honor your name for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will thank you, Lord my God, with all my heart, with the whole of it, and I will honor your name for ever.
verses.directors_commentary: The vow that follows the petition: with the heart united, the thanks can be whole. 'With all my heart' (בכל לבבי) picks up the 'heart' of verse 11, so the vow depends on the previous prayer, as Radak says. The verb אודך is Hiphil of ידה, which means to confess or acknowledge aloud, so 'praise' (KJV) is right in spirit but misses that thanks is public speech. 'Honor your name' (אכבדה שמך) answers the nations in verse 9 who 'honor' the name: the speaker promises to do what he said they would. Ibn Ezra notes the extra 'for ever' that the nations did not receive. Malbim says thanks given only to get more is not 'with all the heart'. Close the scene on a steady, level voice.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of ידה: 'I will acknowledge, thank, confess', a public speaking-out. Translators render both 'thank' and 'praise'.
'For ever, to the age'; Ibn Ezra notes this is added to David's vow beyond what the nations do in verse 9.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to you

verses.translation_literal: For your covenant loyalty is great over me, and you have delivered my life from Sheol, the lowest.
verses.translation_dramatic: For your faithful love is vast, and it lies over me like a sky. You have drawn my life up out of Sheol, out of the deepest pit of it, the place below all places.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse turns on the word "for". After the vow of thanks in verse 12, the singer gives his reason, and it is a fact already won: the deliverance is stated as done ("you have delivered"), though the rest of the psalm still begs for rescue. Play it as a man who stands in the shadow of his past rescue and uses it as proof that he can ask again. Some commentators read the perfect verb as the rescue from enemies and from Saul (Radak on 86:13), while Meiri reads it as the future, so the singer may be speaking of what he is sure will come.

The KJV's "lowest hell" is the main trap. The Hebrew is Sheol, the underworld of the dead, a place of silence and dust. It is not the hell of later Christian imagination. Its "lowest" part is the deepest pit, the place furthest from God's reach, and YLT and ASV keep "Sheol" here. The KJV's "mercy" for חֶסֶד also thins a word of covenant, a loyalty that holds to a bond even when the weaker partner has failed. Later readers did hear a moral rescue in the line: Rashi has David delivered from the depths where adulterers are put, by Nathan's word that the Lord had passed his sin away, and Metzudat David has the same. Malbim splits the verse into good done to the body and to the soul. The verb is a plain one for snatching someone out of danger, and the Hebrew puts the preposition "over" (עָלַי) where English says "toward": the loyalty rests on him from above.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, the faithful love that keeps a bond. English 'mercy' (KJV) loses the covenant sense, and 'kindness' softens it. Metzudat David glosses the next phrase 'you have magnified loyalty to me' (הגדלת עמי חסד), reading גדול עלי as a kindness done for the singer.

'From Sheol, the lowest.' The adjective is feminine to agree with Sheol, and Ibn Ezra takes it as a description of Sheol. Radak notes that all of Sheol is already low, so 'lowest' adds emphasis, and he adds that some take it as Gehinnom. Metzudat Zion glosses תחתיה as depth and lowliness.

verses.translation_literal: O God, arrogant ones have risen up against me, and a company of ruthless ones have sought my life, and they have not set you before them.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, the proud have risen against me. A pack of the ruthless has come hunting my life, and not one of them has set you before his eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns from thanksgiving back to danger, and the actor should let the fear return. Two groups of attackers are named. The zedim are the arrogant, those who act with presumption and contempt (Radak: they pursue David willingly, 'in zadon', by choice, not under compulsion); the 'aritzim are the ruthless, the terrifying ones, from a root of fear and force (Metzudat Zion links it to 'a God feared', el na'aratz). The 'company' (adat) is the word used for an assembly, even Israel's own congregation, here bent into a mob.

The KJV's 'the proud' is acceptable but 'assemblies of violent men' pluralizes a singular word and adds 'men' that Hebrew does not say. 'Sought my life' (bikshu nafshi) is a hunting idiom: they look for it as one looks for prey. The charge of the last clause is theological, not merely moral: 'they have not set you before them' means they act as if God were not watching. In the ancient world a witness or a judge stood 'in front of' the parties; to put him in front is to act as if under his eye. Their crime is a refusal of accountability, not simply cruelty.

philological_notes.note: The arrogant, the presumptuous: those who act deliberately against restraint. Radak stresses that they chase David by free choice, not out of constraint.
The ruthless, the terrifying: tyrants who inspire dread. Metzudat Zion connects the root to fear and strength.
'They have not set you before them': they do not keep God in view, so they feel no accountability. Metzudat David reads it as 'they placed no fear of God before their faces'.

verses.translation_literal: And you, my Lord, [are] a God compassionate and gracious, long of nostrils and great of covenant loyalty and faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, my Lord, you are a God of tender mercy and of grace, slow, so slow, to burn with anger, and vast in loyal love and in truth.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the "they" of verse 14, the psalm turns on "and you" (וְאַתָּה). The proud and the violent set no God before them, and the singer sets before him this description of who God is. The words are a creed, and they reach back to the Lord's self-description at Sinai (Exod 34:6). Say them slowly, almost as a recital, because the singer is quoting back to God the thing God said of himself.

The KJV's "longsuffering" hides the Hebrew picture. אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם is literally 'long of nostrils': in Hebrew anger shows in the hot breath of the nose, so a long nose means a long time before the heat comes. The KJV also reads "a God full of compassion", but the adjectives say a compassionate and gracious God, and רַחוּם shares its root with the word for the womb, a mother's tenderness. BBE's "wisdom" for אֱמֶת is a mistranslation; the word is faithfulness, reliability, a thing that holds when leaned on. Radak hears the אֱמֶת in the last pair as the truth toward David, God's keeping of the word of kingship to him (Radak on 86:15). Malbim says that each attribute is answered by a petition in the following verse: compassion, grace, truth, loyalty.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'long of nostrils', the idiom for patience. Anger is pictured as breath burning through the nose, and 'long' puts off the heat. Radak applies it to the singer: if he sins, God's anger is held back until he fully repents.

'And faithfulness': reliability, trustworthiness, as against the abstract 'truth' of the KJV. The pair with חֶסֶד makes the formula a promise kept. Radak reads God's emet toward David as the keeping of the word of kingship.

verses.translation_literal: Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn your face to me. Show me grace. Give your strength to your servant; save the son of your servant-girl.
verses.directors_commentary:
Having recited the divine name, David makes his demand, and the verbs come in short commands: turn, be gracious, give, save. 'Turn to me' (peneh elai) is the language of the face: God is asked to turn from what occupies him and look at the speaker (Radak's picture is a man turning from his business to attend to one matter). The KJV's 'have mercy upon me' for chonneni is a little loose; the root is grace, favour freely shown.

The closing phrase 'son of your maidservant' is a statement of status. In the ancient household, a child born to a slave woman was born into the house and belonged to the master from the cradle: Rashi calls him a 'yelid bayit', one raised in the master's lap, more bound than one bought with money. David presents himself as a house-born servant who has never known any other master, with a claim on that master's protection; Radak adds that it is the mother who shapes the child, so he is his God's servant by birth and by habit. The KJV's 'handmaid' is an old word that softens the social fact; amah is a female slave or bondwoman. Strength ('oz) is given to a servant to endure, and 'save' (hoshi'ah) is the root that gives us Hoshea and Yeshua.

philological_notes.note: 'Son of your maidservant': a house-born slave, the strongest claim of belonging and dependence. Rashi: he is more bound to his master than a purchased slave.
'Your strength': the power that God has and can give to the weak.

verses.translation_literal: Do with me a sign for good, and let those who hate me see and be ashamed, for you, YHWH, have helped me and have comforted me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Work a sign with me, a sign for good, so that those who hate me will see it and be put to shame. For you, LORD, have been my help; you have been my comfort.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends with a request for something visible. An 'ot' is a sign or token, in Scripture a public mark of divine favour, like the rainbow, the staff that budded, or a miracle given to Gideon; here it is a sign that the haters can read. The KJV's 'shew me a token' is archaic: 'token' once meant exactly this, but a modern ear hears a trinket. 'Do with me' (aseh immi) is the Hebrew's more intimate idiom: a sign made with and alongside him, in his own company. Notice also that the end is shame, not destruction. In an honour-and-shame culture, enemies are defeated when they are made to look foolish before the community.

For the 'sign', tradition has specific readings: Rashi, Malbim and the Targum see it as the day Solomon brought the Ark into the Holy of Holies and the gates opened, a public proof that God had forgiven David; Radak takes it as the kingship itself. The reason clause grounds the request in past experience: 'you have helped me and comforted me'. The KJV's 'holpen' is an old past participle of help. The last verb, nicham, is to console after grief, to restore breath; the sorrow is acknowledged and then answered.

philological_notes.note: A sign, token or marker: visible proof of an invisible fact. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'siman umofet', sign and wonder.
'And let them be ashamed': to be put to shame, disgraced, publicly shown wrong. In this world, shame is the loss of standing before others.
'And you have comforted me': the piel of nacham, to console and bring relief after grief. Ibn Ezra: from the troubles that passed over me.
